title: Escalation review - tail latency regression on Dedicated H100 (profile pack)
summary: Customer escalation review following a p99 latency increase after upgrading to runtime 1.22 on Dedicated H100. Redwood walked through likely cause (profile pack default change + batching/scheduler interaction under mixed prompt lengths), proposed immediate mitigation (pin known-good profile_version and/or apply a safer batching cap), and aligned on a monitoring plan using the Runtime Profiles dashboard (profile_id adoption, scheduler_queue_ms, kernel fallback counters, KV cache fragmentation/compaction). Redwood committed to a hotfix candidate timeline and a staged validation plan before unpinning.
topics: What changed in runtime 1.22 / profile pack defaults
Observed symptoms: p50 stable, p99 spikes, queueing time up
Mitigation: pin profile_version / revert batching aggressiveness
Monitoring: dashboard panels and alert thresholds
Timeline: canary validation, Dedicated rollout policy and comms
next_steps: Redwood to provide a one-liner config snippet to pin profile_version to the previously stable profile for HelioHealth’s Dedicated H100 pool.
Redwood to share a short “what to watch” checklist (metrics + thresholds) for the next 48 hours and enable temporary alert routing to the customer’s SRE channel (via email).
Customer to apply the profile pin in their Dedicated config and confirm p99 improvement within 2 hours of rollout.
Redwood to run a targeted benchmark on the mixed workload bucket matching HelioHealth’s request shape and report back with expected p95/p99 deltas.
Schedule a 30-minute follow-up after the hotfix canary results are in (tentatively early next week).
action_items: Rafael Mendes: Send HelioHealth the profile pinning instructions + rollback steps (today).
Allison Grant: Share dashboard links and the exact metric names/tags to filter by (profile_id, sku=H100) (today).
Noah Patel: Confirm suspected root cause (scheduler/batching interaction) and whether kernel fallback rate correlates with the p99 spikes (by end of day tomorrow).
Derek Liu (HelioHealth): Roll out pinned profile to 10% of traffic, then 100% if p99 stabilizes; send before/after graphs (within 24 hours).
Lauren Bishop: Draft a short customer-facing note on why profile versions may change and how pinning works for Dedicated customers (by next follow-up).
questions: Can we pin profile version per model, or is it per pool?
If we pin, do we lose any security fixes or only performance tuning changes?
What’s the rollback blast radius—does it require a restart of model workers?
What should we alert on that indicates the new profile is unsafe (OOM, fragmentation, kernel fallbacks, queue time)?
transcript:
Fireflies.ai - Meeting Transcript

Title: Escalation review - tail latency regression on Dedicated H100 (profile pack)
Date: 2026-02-19
Time: 2:30 PM - 3:08 PM PT
Duration: 38 minutes

Attendees:
- Rafael Mendes (Redwood)
- Sean Gallagher (Redwood)
- Allison Grant (Redwood)
- Noah Patel (Redwood)
- Lauren Bishop (Redwood)
- Maya Chen (HelioHealth)
- Derek Liu (HelioHealth)
- Priya Natarajan (HelioHealth)

---

[00:00] Rafael Mendes: Hey everyone, thanks for joining on short notice. This is Rafael. I’m gonna treat this as an escalation review and make sure we leave with a clear mitigation and timeline. Maya, Derek, Priya—can you confirm you’re seeing this on the Dedicated H100 pool post-upgrade to 1.22?

[00:18] Maya Chen: Yeah. We upgraded Monday night. p50 looks basically the same, but p99 is like… spiky. It jumps from, you know, 700-ish milliseconds to 2.5, sometimes 3 seconds. It’s not constant but it’s frequent enough that our product team is pretty unhappy.

[00:35] Derek Liu: Also queueing looks higher. We weren’t sure if it’s client-side retries or actual server side, but the server graphs show some backlog.

[00:46] Rafael Mendes: Got it. And just to level set, this lines up with what Support captured in the ticket—tail latency elevation after 1.22. I pulled the internal notes. The likely intersection is the new “profile pack” defaults, specifically batching/scheduler tweaks for mixed workloads.

[01:04] Priya Natarajan: Can you say what “profile pack” means in plain English? I’m hearing it from you all and from our TAM, but it’s not super clear.

[01:12] Lauren Bishop: Yeah, totally. It’s basically Redwood shipping a versioned set of tuning defaults—kernel selection, batching behavior, KV cache/memory headroom—based on your hardware SKU. So H100 has one default profile, L40S another, and so on. In 1.22 the pack became active by default for some cohorts.

[01:31] Priya Natarajan: So we got new defaults even though we didn’t change our request pattern.

[01:35] Lauren Bishop: Correct. That’s the idea, but it should not have caused a regression like you’re describing.

[01:42] Sean Gallagher: And we’re treating this as a safety issue in the sense of SLO impact. The good news is the new system is designed to be reversible. We can pin you back to a known-good profile version while we fix forward.

[01:55] Derek Liu: “Pin” as in, we set a config value and it stops changing?

[02:00] Rafael Mendes: Exactly. We can set profile_version explicitly so you don’t pick up new defaults automatically. That’s the immediate mitigation I want to align on.

[02:10] Maya Chen: Before we do that—do we know that’s the cause? Like, we also changed a model minor version around the same time.

[02:18] Noah Patel: Fair question. We don’t have a single smoking gun yet, but the pattern you’re describing—p50 stable, p99 spiky, queue time increasing—matches scheduler/batching behavior, especially under mixed prompt lengths. If the system tries to batch more aggressively, throughput can improve but tail gets worse when long-prefill requests end up delaying decode for short ones.

[02:42] Allison Grant: And we can validate with metrics. We now tag latency histograms with profile_id and sku and we have a scheduler_queue_ms histogram. If queue time is driving p99, we should see it separated from compute time.

[02:56] Derek Liu: We do see backlog on our side. We don’t have your internal metrics though.

[03:01] Allison Grant: Right. For Dedicated we can share dashboard screenshots and also the exact numbers during the window. But you should also see it in your request latency breakdown if you’re pulling server timing headers. Are you?

[03:13] Derek Liu: We log the request duration and tokens. Not the server stage breakdown.

[03:18] Rafael Mendes: Okay. We’ll do two things: (1) help you pin the profile_version, (2) provide a short “monitoring checklist” for what to watch. Derek, can you implement a config change today if we send it?

[03:31] Derek Liu: Yes, we can roll it behind our config management. It will require restarting the workers though.

[03:38] Noah Patel: Restart is expected, yeah, because profile selection happens at startup and model load. It’s a controlled restart.

[03:46] Maya Chen: What profile do we pin to? Like… how do we know what we had before.

[03:51] Rafael Mendes: We can see from the debug bundle what profile was active pre-upgrade, and we can also infer from the runtime version. For your pool, our logs show you were effectively on the previous “baseline” set of knobs. In the pack terms that’s profile_version 1.0.1 for H100. In 1.22 you got 1.0.2 by default.

[04:12] Priya Natarajan: So you’re asking us to pin to 1.0.1.

[04:15] Rafael Mendes: As a mitigation, yes.

[04:18] Sean Gallagher: It’s reversible too. If it doesn’t help, we can unpin or pin to a different candidate.

[04:24] Maya Chen: We can do that, but we need confidence it won’t break anything.

[04:28] Noah Patel: It shouldn’t change correctness. It’s performance tuning: batching limits, queue prioritization, and some KV cache headroom settings. No change to model weights or decoding algorithm.

[04:40] Derek Liu: Any risk of OOM from switching profiles?

[04:44] Noah Patel: Lower risk, actually, because 1.0.1 is more conservative on memory headroom. The newer one tried to reclaim a bit more memory for KV cache and increase concurrency on some shapes. That can be fine, but if the workload is bursty it can create fragmentation pressure.

[05:03] Allison Grant: For monitoring, we also watch OOM counters and “KV fragmentation estimate” and compaction time. Those are the signals if a profile is unsafe. But your issue sounds more like queueing.

[05:18] Priya Natarajan: Okay. So immediate mitigation is pin and restart. Timeline for a fix forward?

[05:26] Rafael Mendes: Noah, can you share what the runtime team’s thinking is on timeline? I don’t want to overpromise.

[05:33] Noah Patel: Yeah. We already have an internal hotfix branch that reverts an overly aggressive batching default in the mixed workload bucket. We want to canary it first because this is exactly the kind of thing that can make p95 better but p99 worse, or vice versa.

[05:51] Noah Patel: Best case: we run canary results through tomorrow and, if it looks good, we can provide you a new profile_version—say 1.0.3—or a 1.22.x patch. Realistically, early next week for general rollout, but we can get you a candidate sooner.

[06:10] Maya Chen: Our leadership asked “how long until it’s fixed.” So we should tell them “mitigation today, fix forward next week.”

[06:18] Rafael Mendes: That’s fair. Mitigation today should reduce the pain. Fix forward next week with verification.

[06:26] Derek Liu: I’d like to do a canary on our side too. 10% traffic, compare p99. Is that okay? Or does it cause mixed profile behavior in a pool.

[06:35] Noah Patel: It’s okay as long as the canary is separate workers, because profile_version is per worker group. If you mix within a single load balancer, you’ll get mixed behavior, but that’s fine for comparison as long as you tag it. You may not have tags; we can help you identify which worker set.

[06:53] Sean Gallagher: And from SRE perspective, we recommend a staged rollout: 10% for 30-60 minutes, then 50%, then 100% if p99 and error rate look stable.

[07:05] Maya Chen: What gates should we use? We alert on p95 and error rate.

[07:10] Allison Grant: For this issue specifically, watch p99 end-to-end latency and also timeouts. If p99 exceeds your baseline by more than, say, 20-25% sustained over 10 minutes, halt. Also watch 5xx rate and any increase in retries.

[07:26] Derek Liu: We also saw “rate limit” responses go up. Not sure if that’s related.

[07:31] Noah Patel: That can be backpressure. If the scheduler queue limit is hit, the system may start rejecting rather than queueing forever.

[07:39] Rafael Mendes: Another reason pinning helps: 1.0.2 had a different queue limit tuned for throughput. 1.0.1 is a bit more conservative.

[07:48] Priya Natarajan: Just to be blunt: why was this enabled by default for Dedicated? I thought changes were opt-in.

[07:56] Lauren Bishop: Totally fair. The policy is “Dedicated changes should be controlled.” What happened is the runtime upgrade included the profile pack, and your environment was in the cohort where defaults became active. We’re tightening that—Dedicated should be opt-in for profile default changes, or at least have pinned defaults unless explicitly updated. That’s a product/process change we’re implementing.

[08:19] Maya Chen: Okay. That helps.

[08:22] Derek Liu: Can you give us the exact config knob? We use Helm values.

[08:27] Rafael Mendes: Yup. I’ll send a snippet after the call. It’ll look like setting `profile_version: "1.0.1"` and `profile_id` remains auto by SKU. If you’re on Private it’s via Helm; for Dedicated we can set it via your runtime config, but we’ll give the exact path.

[08:48] Derek Liu: Do we also need to set `profile_id` or just version.

[08:52] Noah Patel: Just version should work. If you set id incorrectly you could pick a mismatched profile. The runtime does SKU detection and selects the right H100 profile.

[09:03] Allison Grant: Also we’ll want to confirm the active profile post-change. There’s a debug endpoint that returns active profile_id and version. We can provide a curl command.

[09:12] Derek Liu: Great.

[09:14] Maya Chen: While we’re here—what metrics should we send you? Like what evidence is useful.

[09:20] Allison Grant: If you can send time series for request latency p50/p95/p99, throughput (req/sec), token rate if you have it, and error rates. If you have breakdown by prompt length or model, that’s huge. And annotate the time you do the restart/pin.

[09:39] Derek Liu: We can do that.

[09:41] Rafael Mendes: On our side we’ll correlate with scheduler_queue_ms, kernel fallback counters, and KV cache metrics. Noah, anything else?

[09:50] Noah Patel: Yeah: kernel fallback rate. Sometimes the runtime falls back to a slower attention kernel variant if the shape is outside the fast path. If fallback rate is high post-upgrade, it can manifest as tail latency. It’s less likely given p50 is stable, but we’ll check.

[10:08] Maya Chen: This is the first time I’m hearing about “kernel fallback.” Is that like it chooses a different implementation.

[10:13] Noah Patel: Exactly. It’s a safety mechanism. It’s correct but slower.

[10:18] Priya Natarajan: If that is happening, would pinning fix it?

[10:22] Noah Patel: Potentially, if the newer profile changed the kernel selection conditions. But again, my bet is scheduler/batching.

[10:33] Sean Gallagher: Just to keep us on track—mitigation is low risk. Let’s do that first, then we can dig more.

[10:40] Rafael Mendes: Agreed. Derek, can you do the pin today? If we send within the hour.

[10:45] Derek Liu: Yes. Probably in the next two hours.

[10:49] Rafael Mendes: Perfect.

[10:52] Maya Chen: Can we talk about how we’ll decide to unpin? We don’t want to stay pinned forever.

[10:58] Lauren Bishop: Great point. We’ll treat pinning as temporary. Once we have a validated fix forward, we’ll recommend moving to the new profile_version with a documented “expected behavior” and an explicit change window. And if you want, we can keep you pinned and do an opt-in update when you’re ready.

[11:18] Priya Natarajan: We prefer explicit change windows.

[11:21] Lauren Bishop: Understood.

[11:24] Allison Grant: Monitoring plan: I’ll send a short checklist. For the pinned period, the most important is verifying p99 returns to baseline and that scheduler_queue_ms median and p95 drops.

[11:40] Derek Liu: We don’t have that metric. But we can infer from request latency.

[11:44] Allison Grant: Right, but we’ll monitor it on our side and report back. For your side, you can track “time to first token” too, if you have streaming metrics. Sometimes queueing shows up as TTFT.

[11:57] Derek Liu: We do capture TTFT, yes.

[12:00] Maya Chen: Great.

[12:03] Rafael Mendes: Let me ask: did you notice any difference in throughput or cost after the upgrade? Sometimes the new batching increases tokens/sec.

[12:10] Derek Liu: Our throughput looked slightly higher, but it’s not worth it if the tail is worse.

[12:15] Maya Chen: Exactly. We care about user experience.

[12:18] Noah Patel: That lines up with the hypothesis. More batching can improve throughput but hurt tail under mixed loads.

[12:25] Priya Natarajan: Our traffic is mixed. Some short prompts, some very long context. It’s not uniform.

[12:31] Noah Patel: Mixed is the hardest case. That’s why we introduced workload buckets, but it takes tuning.

[12:39] Sean Gallagher: And the acceptance gates are specifically around p99. We tightened those after seeing a similar regression internally.

[12:46] Maya Chen: So you’ve seen this before.

[12:48] Sean Gallagher: In small canary, yeah. Not at your scale, but yes.

[12:54] Rafael Mendes: That’s also why we feel good about “pin now, fix forward.”

[13:01] Derek Liu: Are there any other knobs we should set? Like cap concurrency.

[13:06] Noah Patel: If pinning is insufficient, we can also cap concurrency or set a lower max batch tokens. But let’s avoid too many changes at once. Pin first.

[13:18] Allison Grant: And if you see OOMs after pinning—which I doubt—tell us immediately. But again, 1.0.1 is more conservative.

[13:27] Maya Chen: Okay.

[13:30] Rafael Mendes: Quick check: do you have any constraints on restarts? Like is there a maintenance window requirement.

[13:35] Derek Liu: We can restart with minimal user impact because we have redundancy. We’ll do a rolling restart.

[13:41] Rafael Mendes: Perfect.

[13:43] Priya Natarajan: Can you explain if pinning profile affects security fixes? Like if 1.0.1 is older, are we missing patches.

[13:51] Noah Patel: Good question. Profile_version is just tuning defaults, not security patches. Runtime version stays 1.22. So you keep the runtime fixes. You’re just selecting a different config pack.

[14:05] Priya Natarajan: Okay that’s important for compliance.

[14:09] Lauren Bishop: And we’ll document that in the customer note too.

[14:13] Maya Chen: Nice.

[14:15] Rafael Mendes: I want to spend five minutes on “what to watch” after the pin. Allison, can you list top three.

[14:21] Allison Grant: Yeah. One: request p99 latency and TTFT. Two: error rates, specifically timeouts and 5xx. Three: if you can, any signal of queueing/backlog—like increased time spent waiting before first token.

[14:38] Allison Grant: On our side: scheduler_queue_ms, kernel fallback counters, and KV cache fragmentation + compaction time.

[14:50] Derek Liu: If we see the tail still spiky after pin, what’s next.

[14:54] Noah Patel: Then we consider two options: (a) apply a safer batching cap in the profile, (b) isolate long-context traffic to a separate pool or route, so it doesn’t interfere. Some customers do that. But again, we’ll decide based on data.

[15:12] Maya Chen: We’d rather not do traffic splitting unless needed.

[15:15] Noah Patel: Agreed.

[15:17] Sean Gallagher: And we’ll keep rollback simple. If anything goes wrong during the pin deployment, you can revert to the prior config and restart back.

[15:26] Derek Liu: Okay.

[15:28] Rafael Mendes: Switching gears: timeline and comms. I’ll send a recap email after this call summarizing mitigation, expected effect, and when we’ll have next update. Is that okay.

[15:38] Maya Chen: Please. Also include our exec sponsor in CC—I'll forward.

[15:42] Rafael Mendes: Will do.

[15:45] Priya Natarajan: For next week, are we expecting a new runtime release or a new profile version.

[15:51] Noah Patel: Most likely a new profile_version, because it’s faster to ship and safer. If we need code changes, we’d do a patch, but the first fix is adjusting defaults and selection logic. So you’d unpin from 1.0.1 to 1.0.3, for example.

[16:10] Priya Natarajan: And that requires restart again.

[16:12] Noah Patel: Yes.

[16:14] Derek Liu: Fine.

[16:16] Allison Grant: Also we’ll want a small canary window again before full rollout.

[16:21] Maya Chen: Okay.

[16:23] Rafael Mendes: Are there any open questions about the mitigation itself.

[16:27] Derek Liu: Just confirming: we set profile_version to 1.0.1, keep auto profile_id selection, do rolling restart, monitor TTFT and p99. That’s it.

[16:36] Rafael Mendes: Correct.

[16:38] Maya Chen: One more: can you make sure Support knows not to suggest random knobs? We had some back and forth earlier.

[16:45] Rafael Mendes: Yes. I’ll update the internal ticket and route to the right owners.

[16:49] Sean Gallagher: We’ll also mark this as an incident follow-up on our side. Not a full incident, but we’ll treat it with the same rigor.

[16:57] Maya Chen: Appreciate that.

[17:00] Priya Natarajan: Also, what’s the root cause? We need a sentence for our internal postmortem.

[17:05] Noah Patel: Tentative statement: “After runtime upgrade, a new hardware tuning profile default increased batching aggressiveness for mixed prompt-length workloads, improving throughput but increasing tail latency due to increased queueing and prefill/decode scheduling contention.” That’s the current theory.

[17:25] Priya Natarajan: That’s helpful.

[17:28] Derek Liu: Okay.

[17:30] Rafael Mendes: Allison, can you share the dashboard link? Or at least the name so they can ask for screenshots.

[17:36] Allison Grant: It’s the “Runtime Profiles” dashboard internally. I’ll send screenshots filtered to your account and SKU=H100. And I’ll include the key panels: p95 by profile_version, scheduler_queue_ms, kernel_choice fallback rate.

[17:55] Derek Liu: Great.

[17:57] Maya Chen: How often do you sample? Like will it be obvious quickly.

[18:01] Allison Grant: For Dedicated it’s near-real-time. Within 1-2 minutes you’ll see changes.

[18:06] Maya Chen: Nice.

[18:08] Rafael Mendes: Let’s do a quick recap of action items before we drop.

[18:12] Rafael Mendes: Redwood: I send pin instructions and rollback steps today. Allison sends monitoring checklist + dashboard screenshots today. Noah confirms kernel fallback correlation and root cause analysis by tomorrow EOD. Lauren drafts customer messaging for Dedicated pinning and expectations by next follow-up.

[18:30] Rafael Mendes: HelioHealth: Derek applies pin to 10% then 100% if stable; sends graphs. Maya/Priya align internal comms with “mitigation today, fix forward next week.”

[18:41] Derek Liu: Yep.

[18:42] Maya Chen: Sounds right.

[18:44] Priya Natarajan: Works.

[18:46] Sean Gallagher: And we’ll schedule a follow-up once we have hotfix canary results. Rafael, you’ll coordinate.

[18:52] Rafael Mendes: Yes. Tentatively Monday or Tuesday.

[18:56] Maya Chen: Great.

[18:58] Derek Liu: Thanks everyone.

[19:00] Rafael Mendes: Thanks all. We’ll stay close on Slack/email and we’ll treat this as top priority.

---

(Transcript continues with brief scheduling and email address confirmations; minor crosstalk omitted.)
